purpose: NASA records evaluated for the platform outside the Biomass Production Chamber report set: one light-quality study with measured endpoints for the exact crops the simulator models, and one ethylene-sensitivity study that defines a closed-chamber risk the model does not carry.

20160006559.label: NASA/KSC light-quality study
20160006559.title: Comparative Study of Lettuce and Radish Grown Under Red and Blue LEDs and White Fluorescent Lamps
20160006559.authors: M. A. Mickens, G. Massa, G. Newsham, R. Wheeler, M. Birmele
20160006559.dataNature: Ground-based growth-chamber experiment at equal PPF; measured endpoints for lettuce and radish, the two crops the platform simulates. Not a spaceflight experiment.
20160006559.whyItMatters: Answers the platform's weakest evidence row (light spectrum is recorded as an annotation). It gives an equal-PPF comparison of red+blue LEDs against white fluorescent light for the same crops, from NASA, with n and SD printed.
20160006559.abstract: Two short-cycle crops, red romaine lettuce (Lactuca sativa cv. Outredgeous) and radish (Raphanus sativa cv. Cherry Bomb), were grown under either red (630 nm) + blue (450 nm) LEDs or daylight tri-phosphor fluorescent lamps at equal photosynthetic photon flux, and compared for fresh biomass, morphology, leaf area, chlorophyll and ATP. Measured endpoints are on the poster's Table 1, not machine-readable text.

measurementPages.excerpt: PPF was maintained at ~200 umol m-2 s-1 for both crops. The photoperiod was 18 h of active light, and 6 h of darkness. Chamber air temperature, relative humidity, and CO2 levels were maintained at 23 C, 70 %, and 1200 umol mol-1, respectively.

In FL light, lettuce exhibited increased shoot dimensions, leaf area, and fresh biomass in comparison to the RB treatment, but there were no significant differences in lettuce chlorophyll content. For radish, the RB treatment appeared to enhance leaf/root growth while the additional wavelengths from the FL treatment triggered more biomass accumulation in the root storage... Although the total fresh mass was not significantly different under either treatment, the light quality affected how the biomass was distributed in the plant.

structured.label: Table 1 (poster p.1) - effects of light quality on shoot length, diameter, fresh mass, leaf area and chlorophyll content, n = 20, +/- = SD
structured.read_from: rendered poster page, not a text layer
quality_notes: Significance symbols are reproduced as printed (*** ** * NS); the poster does not print the alpha levels.
Poster text is a raster image: there is no text layer to quote from, so the values were read off the rendered page and the rendered region is hash-pinned instead (region.pixels_sha256).
n = 20 plants per crop per treatment; two replications of pots.

limits: One chamber, one cultivar per crop, one campaign; two treatments only (no green-only or far-red arm).
Ground-based; says nothing about reduced gravity, the Moon or Mars.
Endpoints are fresh mass and morphology at harvest, not a spectral response curve: there is no measured yield-versus-wavelength surface to fit.
The poster prints significance symbols but not alpha levels or the test used.

20040087496.label: Ethylene sensitivity study
20040087496.title: Sensitivity of wheat and rice to low levels of atmospheric ethylene
20040087496.dataNature: Peer-reviewed closed-chamber study of a trace gas that accumulates in sealed plant growth chambers. NTRS lists no downloadable full text, so only the published abstract is used.
20040087496.whyItMatters: SpaceAgriSim models a sealed habitat and has no ethylene term at all. This record quantifies how large that omission can be (36-63 % yield loss at 50 ppb), which is a gap the platform must disclose rather than silently ignore.
20040087496.abstract: Ethylene (C2H4) is produced throughout the life cycle of plants and can accumulate in closed growth chambers to levels 100 times higher than outside. Continuous C2H4 from 0 to 1000 nmol mol-1 was applied over whole life cycles: yield was reduced by 36 % in wheat and 63 % in rice at 50 nmol mol-1, and both species were virtually sterile at 1000 nmol mol-1. Exposure stopped at anthesis reduced yield much less, so the damage is concentrated around seed set. In two further greenhouse studies at 50 nmol mol-1 and 350/1200/5000 micromol mol-1 CO2, USU-Apogee wheat was not significantly affected while Super Dwarf was reduced by 60 %, and elevated CO2 did not change ethylene sensitivity.

abstract_statements.statement: yield reduced 36 % in wheat at 50 ppb continuous ethylene
yield reduced 63 % in rice at 50 ppb continuous ethylene
both species virtually sterile at 1000 ppb continuous
exposure stopped at anthesis gave much smaller yield reductions
Super Dwarf wheat yield reduced 60 % at 50 ppb in the greenhouse
USU-Apogee wheat not significantly reduced at 50 ppb
elevated CO2 (350/1200/5000 ppm) did not change ethylene sensitivity

limits: Abstract only: NTRS exposes no full text for this record, so no page-level quote is possible.
Wheat and rice in ground chambers/greenhouses - not lettuce, tomato or radish, and not a space habitat.
The platform deliberately does NOT turn this into an ethylene yield factor: a single crop pair at one trace-gas range is not a transferable response surface.

not_used.reason: The light-quality endpoints are recorded and citable, but no spectral response coefficient is fitted: two treatments cannot define a wavelength-to-yield curve, and the platform records spectrum as an annotation on purpose.
Ethylene is disclosed as an unmodelled closed-chamber risk. Adding a factor from one abstract would be a fabricated coefficient.
